source.title: On the Maximum Hessian Eigenvalue and Generalization
source.authors: Simran Kaur; Jérémy E. Cohen; Zachary Chase Lipton

record.file_problem: none; full paper text including appendix is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study varies training interventions and measures test accuracy and the maximum Hessian eigenvalue, using those measurements to assess whether the eigenvalue tracks generalization. It does not use the magnitude-aware perturbation measure named in V7.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own VGG, Fixup ResNet, and MLP experiments. Values displayed only in plots are not reconstructed; rows use explicit textual comparisons from the paper.
record.test_reason: The Fashion-MNIST experiments directly test dropout's effect on held-out accuracy in a two-hidden-layer MLP, extending V6 to a new dataset. The Hessian experiments do not test V7's magnitude-aware perturbation measure, and training to 99% accuracy does not test V5's fixed-epoch comparison.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that maximum Hessian eigenvalues do not reliably explain generalization improvements: interventions can lower them without improving test accuracy, and batch normalization can improve accuracy without consistently lowering them. They explicitly limit this conclusion to this flatness metric.
record.recipe_differences: The study measures maximum Hessian eigenvalue and test accuracy under learning-rate, batch-size, SAM, dropout, and batch-normalization interventions; it does not reproduce the original studies' methods.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary with batch size and learning rate; SAM results also vary with batch normalization. Dropout outcomes depend on dropout probability.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger learning rates reduce maximum Hessian eigenvalues even when their test-accuracy benefits plateau at large batch sizes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unscaled maximum Hessian eigenvalues do not consistently track generalization across learning-rate and batch-size settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Jointly scaling batch size and learning rate can preserve test accuracy while changing maximum Hessian eigenvalues.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Equivalent test accuracy can coexist with different unscaled Hessian sharpness.

fits_no_version.finding: SAM reduces maximum Hessian eigenvalues while its test-accuracy effects depend on batch size and batch normalization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAM-induced reductions in unscaled Hessian sharpness do not uniformly improve generalization.

fits_no_version.finding: Batch normalization changes test accuracy despite similar maximum Hessian eigenvalues, with the accuracy difference changing direction across learning rates.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Batch normalization's generalization effects need not be accompanied by corresponding changes in unscaled Hessian sharpness.

record.problems: Many results are presented in plots without exact numeric values in the text; the paper notes λmax is calculated over a subset of the training dataset due to compute constraints. The BN VGG experiment averages 4 runs; the BN VGG SAM experiment uses one fixed-seed run.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows were created for every plotted learning-rate, batch-size, or ρ point because the supplied text gives no exact per-point values; textual aggregate comparisons are recorded instead. Figure 3's batch-size sweep and Figure 15's GELU replication have figure-only values and no additional explicit per-setting comparisons beyond the reported trends.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting, chance-level random-label test accuracy, and coexistence with natural-label generalization.
Width beyond interpolation and its effect on test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning.
Batch-size effects under a fixed epoch budget and remedies evaluated under that budget.
Convolutional classifiers, very small training sets, training underfitting from excessive dropout, and joint removal of dropout and weight decay with augmentation.

Magnitude-scaled perturbation tolerance, its association with generalization gaps, and its ranking against norm- and margin-based measures. Unscaled maximum Hessian eigenvalues cannot establish these results.
Removal of highly memorized examples versus random removal followed by retraining.

missing.what: A separate large-batch MLP row for improved test accuracy with dropout through p = 0.2, compared with no dropout.
The stated excessive-dropout degradation across both learning rates and both batch regimes; R2 records only the illustrative batch-100, learning-rate-0.1 comparison.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for V6. Its excessive-dropout result is consistent with V6's existing qualification and should not by itself be labeled a new scope limitation. No verdict on V7 follows from these Hessian measurements.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Widening beyond interpolation and its effect on test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image-classifier generalization.
Large-batch versus small-batch performance under a fixed epoch budget.
Very small training sets; removing dropout and weight decay together with augmentation.
Magnitude-scaled weight perturbation tolerance and its ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.

rows.subject: MLP with 2 hidden layers
rows.stage_stated: trained using minibatch SGD until achieving 99% train accuracy
rows.operation_detail: Varied dropout probability, with dropout applied to both hidden layers.
rows.value: Adding dropout (up to p = 0.2) improves generalization.
rows.uncertainty: Averaged over 3 runs with different random seeds; no error bars stated.
rows.note: The paper states this modest-dropout improvement for both small- and large-batch SGD; this row records the small-batch setting.
rows.check: Figure 8 describes the test-accuracy improvements through p = 0.2 as slight; under the stated rules, a small improvement is partial.

source_check.locator_found: Section 3.4, Figure 8 caption and paragraph (i), pp. 9–10.

rows.subject: MLP with 2 hidden layers
rows.stage_stated: trained using minibatch SGD until achieving 99% train accuracy
rows.operation_detail: Compared excessive dropout with a lower dropout probability.
rows.value: The solution found using p = 0.7 generalizes worse.
rows.note: The text says the p = 0.7 solution also has a smaller λmax; the comparison supports the stated excessive-dropout qualification.
rows.check: Worse test accuracy at p = 0.7 supports excessive-dropout degradation, but does not establish V6's underfitting explanation: both conditions are trained to 99% training accuracy. The reversal concerns the benefit of increasing dropout, not the entire qualified version.
